title: One Guru, many sangats
hookLine: the variety of the panth is its breadth, not its weakness

cards: Someone who listened to this whole block might come away with a worry. Blue-robed Nihangs and white-clad Namdharis. Strict ragas and simple tunes.
Meat on one plate, none on another. Arguments over a calendar, a book, the five at the bowl. Isn't a faith with this many streams coming apart at the seams?
It's a fair question, and an honest one. Outsiders ask it, and so, sometimes, do Sikhs themselves. Today offers another way to see the same picture.

teach.b: Start with what doesn't vary. The Sikh streams this block visited bow to the same Guru Granth Sahib, and the Mool Mantar at its opening names one Creator for all of them. So the sangats are many, and the Guru is one.
Now look at the variety again, from the center outward. A banyan tree drops roots from its branches until a single tree looks like a grove.

teach.h: A BANYAN WIDENS TO HOLD MORE SHADE.
teach.b: Its width isn't a sign of trouble; it's how the tree holds more shade.

The panth has spread across villages and cities, castes and continents, warriors and scholars and singers, and each has taken the same Word into a different life. Gurbani gives the reason the spread doesn't scatter it.
In Sohila, the night prayer, Guru Nanak says on Ang 13, here in paraphrase: the one light is in everyone, and that light is the One; by its shining, everyone is lit.
If the same light is in each sangat, then many sangats is simply the light, showing up in many rooms. That doesn't make every disagreement easy; this block has been honest that some are hard.
But breadth means a Sikh who struggles in one sangat can find another under the same Guru. It means a newcomer in Texas and an elder in Amritsar can open the same page.
It means the panth can carry music and martial art, study and service, quiet and loud, without needing them all in one person.

how: Sikhs of many streams gather in their own sangats around the same Guru Granth Sahib, and Sohila, the night prayer with its line on the one light in everyone, is recited before sleep.

games.q: a Sikh finds one sangat hard to belong to. what does the panth's breadth offer?
o: find another sangat under the same Guru.
games.why: many sangats, one Guru: the same Granth is open in each, so another room is always under the same light.

practice: Let the streams you've met come forward one by one with the breath, the warriors, the scholars, the singers, the quiet ones in white, the newcomers explaining things in English, and simply thank each for what it keeps.
Then widen it to the people unlike you who make your world bigger, and if you pray, thank Waheguru for the one light in all of them.

wordCard.voice: One Guru. The Guru Granth Sahib at the center of many sangats: one light, showing up in many rooms. Today's word.
